    Google Adds Pageburst & 11 Other Existing Bots To Its Crawler Docs via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that google identified pageburst as a user agent that renders pages to measure Google Ads quality and landing page safety and ignores robots.txt rules.
    • Pageburst is one of 12 existing user agents Google added to its crawler documentation on Nov.
    • “These crawlers and fetchers are not new; we’re documenting existing high-volume clients that are more likely to show up in server logs and that we’ve received questions about.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that google identified pageburst as a user agent that renders pages to measure Google Ads quality and landing page safety and ignores robots.txt rules. Its two strings look like a browser’s and do not contain “Googlebot”; a bot rule created using “Googlebot” will not capture them.

    Pageburst is one of 12 existing user agents Google added to its crawler documentation on Nov. 23, along with a corrected entry for APIs-Google. Google’s crawling documentation changelog explains:.

    “These crawlers and fetchers are not new; we’re documenting existing high-volume clients that are more likely to show up in server logs and that we’ve received questions about.”.

    The 12 belong to Google products other than Search, such as Google Ads, Gmail and Google Cloud.

    Google’s special-case crawlers page, which lists crawlers used by specific Google products, states pageburst “renders web pages for Google Ads quality, landing-page safety, and page understanding.” The entry adds that “it’s unaffected by crawling preferences.”.

    The desktop string identifies as Chrome on Linux and the mobile one as Chrome for iOS on an iPad, and both include “compatible; pageburst.”.

    AdsBot, which checks web page ad quality for Google Ads, has its own robots.txt token. Pageburst’s entry lists no token and says the user agent “ignores robots.txt rules.”.

    The highlights show what to look for in server logs and where Google states its robots.txt policy.

    Google’s documentation says user-agent strings can be faked. Special-case crawlers use the IP addresses defined in Google’s special-crawlers.json; these have a reverse-DNS match of rate-limited-proxy-***-***-***-***.google.com. The pageburst entry does not say what occurs when a website blocks the Google Ads check.

    Besides pageburst, each of the five other newly documented special-case entries claims the user agent “ignores robots.txt rules.”.

    Industry observers note that google’s user-triggered fetchers page covers the six newly documented fetchers and says that because a user requested the fetch, these fetchers “generally ignore robots.txt rules.” Three of those (AppEngine-Google, Google-Apps-Script and Google-Cloud-Tasks) send requests for code running within Google’s platform-based products. The remaining three are GoogleImageProxy, which is used to load image content into email applications such as Gmail, along with Google Web Preview and the PageSpeed Insights fetcher, both with strings ending in Chrome-Lighthouse.

    Sources indicate that several of the newly listed user agents seem to use standard browser strings. For example, a string from GoogleImageProxy appears similar to Firefox 11 on Windows NT 5.1; the strings for Google Web Preview and PageSpeed Insights, and one of PlayStore-Google’s, were created using Chrome strings. A filter that only identifies “Googlebot” would miss all of these.

    It has been revealed that google has moved APIs-Google, which makes requests to the webhook notification systems developers create within Google Cloud and Google Workspace APIs, from the list of special-case crawlers to the list of user-triggered fetchers. APIs-Google’s push requests, the changelog says, “come from the user-triggered fetcher IP ranges and ignore robots.txt rules.” Google added a missing semicolon after “APIs-Google” in its documented string and tells developers to modify any code that was previously using a hardcoded version of the earlier string.

    Prior to the Nov. 23 update, Google had included robots.txt as a method to block requests from APIs-Google in its documentation. In an Oct. 21 capture, the robots.txt token was present on the special-case page. On Oct. 30, a capture of the APIs-Google page highlighted “Use robots.txt” as one of two methods to block requests from APIs-Google. Now the APIs-Google page states that it “ignores robots.txt rules”; for controlling the delivery of notifications, the page points to either the developer who created the notification system or Google Cloud’s abuse form for unexpected requests.

    In a recent development, pageburst renders pages for ads in Google and does not follow robots.txt. Check for “pageburst” in the log entries for your servers and CDNs, verify with Google’s procedures that the IP addresses are in its special-crawler ranges, and see if your pages were delivered to the verified requests, or if a challenge or a 403 was returned.

    According to recent reports, roger Montti covered Google’s advice on Nov. 18 that general bot blocking may keep Googlebot from crawling content when moving a CDN; the same advice should be applied to other Google clients that do not have the name Googlebot.

    Google’s special-case and user-triggered pages both say their lists aren’t exhaustive and cover the requestors “more likely to show up in log files.” The crawling documentation changelog, which is where Google logs additions like these, has an RSS feed.

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, substantial gainers included W42ST, the Point/Plover Metro Wire, Grice Connect (“In the rural south, death is a large social driver”), and the Philomath News. Here’s our quarterly ranking of the top 25 local for-profit news sites in the United States.

    In a recent development, it’s time for our latest look at which newsrooms are having success increasing their web traffic. We bring you four of these each quarter, looking at four different market segments: local newspapers, nonprofit news outlets, public media stations, and for-profit local news sites. Rankings are based on estimates from Similarweb.

    According to recent reports, today’s edition looks at local for-profit news sites. (Eligible sites for this ranking are for-profit members of the trade group LION Publishers — LION standing for Local, Independent, Online News — so these are mostly digital-born newsrooms, not newspapers or TV stations.) The rankings for Q3 feature many of the same sites that performed well in our last edition. This time around, we’ve got details from local news sites in Latest York, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nevada, Georgia, and Oregon. Below that are the Top 25 rankings for July, August, and September.

    It has been revealed that W42ST In New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July. Publisher Phil O’Brien stated that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST. “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.” O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s currently trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve introduced earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week. It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said. Point/Plover Metro Wire Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski. The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said. Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said. “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she said. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.” Grice Connect Statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July. DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position. But Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site. Philomath News The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath. Similarweb stats demonstrated a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he said. In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said. Oklahoma City Free Press, LINK nky, This Is Reno In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.” The Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews. Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.     It has been revealed that in Latest York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July.

    Industry observers note that publisher Phil O’Brien said that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST.

    In a recent development, “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.”.

    O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s right now trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The upcoming daily newsletter they’ve debuted earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week.

    According to recent reports, it’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he noted.

    Industry observers note that wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski.

    The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski mentioned high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said.

    Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining latest customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said.

    “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she mentioned. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and latest sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.”.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Sources indicate that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    The generational edge that highlights up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

    Ask a 19-year-old how TikTok decides what to show them, and you’ll likely get a fast, confident answer about watch time, likes, and how “the algorithm just gets me.” Ask their grandmother, and you’re more likely to get a shrug.

    Recent findings suggest that the scene fits a story we’ve been telling for years: Young people are “digital natives” who intuitively grasp the platforms they grew up on, while older adults are outsiders, left behind and vulnerable. That story matters more than it used to. Algorithmically curated platforms are now a major source of news for Americans of all ages, which means people’s sense of how those systems work shapes how they judge the information they get there.

    But when you test what each group actually knows, rather than what they say they know, the story doesn’t hold up.

    RELATED ARTICLETrapped by what they know: Young adults’ algorithmic cynicismMyojung ChungNovember 17, 2025In a piece last year for Nieman Lab, I reported that young adults who spent more time on social media tended to know less about how algorithms work, and I speculated that constant use might create an illusion of understanding. My recent study published in Newly introduced Media & Society set out to test that idea directly — measuring not just what people know, but how confident they are about it — across the full adult age range.

    Surveying 1,205 U.S. adults ages 18 to 65 and older, I measured two things. First, I asked people to rate their own understanding of how algorithms select, rank, and personalize content. Second, I measured their actual awareness of how these systems work, which covers content filtering, automated decision-making, data use, and algorithmic bias.

    The self-ratings matched the conventional wisdom: Younger respondents rated their understanding significantly higher than older respondents did. But the awareness scores did not. Across every age group, actual awareness of how algorithms function was essentially flat.

    Industry observers note that in other words, the generational edge that reveals up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

    To capture this, I use the concept “algorithmic knowledge confidence”: the gap between what people believe they know and what they can demonstrate. When self-assessment outpaces actual awareness, that’s overconfidence; when it lags behind, that’s underconfidence. Young adults tended toward the former: They don’t necessarily understand algorithms better, but they feel more certain that they do. Older adults tended toward the latter: They don’t know less, but they’re more cautious about claiming what they know.

    In a recent development, then why would the most-online generation feel the surest? Psychologists have long documented that people mistake familiarity for understanding. When something feels easy to process — often simply because we’ve encountered it many times — we tend to assume we understand it. This is called processing fluency.

    Exposure to social media differs sharply by age. About 95% of 18- to 29-year-olds use YouTube and about 63% use TikTok, according to Pew Research; among adults 65 and older, those figures drop to 64% and 12%. For younger consumers, algorithmic feeds are part of the daily routine, and that routine produces a comfortable sense of “I know how this works,” whether or not it’s true. Older adults, with less exposure, don’t get the same fluency cues, and default to more conservative self-assessments.

    My data are consistent with this explanation. The number of platforms people used daily accounted for a meaningful share of the link between age and overconfidence: The more platforms someone used, the further their self-rated understanding outran their demonstrated awareness. Because this is a survey taken at one point in time, it can’t prove that heavy use causes overconfidence, but the pattern fits the fluency account well.

    This miscalibration isn’t just a matter of bruised egos or modest grandparents. It reveals up in how people evaluate the news and information in their feeds.

    It has been revealed that RELATED ARTICLEWant to fight misinformation? Teach people how algorithms workMyojung ChungSeptember 4, 2024Younger adults who overestimated their algorithmic understanding were more likely to see the content in their feeds as reliable and trustworthy, and more likely to believe they were being exposed to a diverse range of viewpoints. Older adults who underestimated their understanding showed the opposite pattern: more skepticism about the reliability of what they saw, and a sense that their feeds were narrower than they might actually be.

    Other research points in the same direction for younger audiences. A Stanford study found that two-thirds of U.S. high school students couldn’t tell a news article from sponsored content, a reminder that growing up inside algorithmic feeds is no guarantee of being able to evaluate them.

    But the older adults’ pattern isn’t a healthy one either. Blanket distrust is as poor a guide to information as blanket confidence. It can lead people to dismiss accurate reporting along with misinformation, or to disengage from platforms entirely rather than learning to use them critically.

    First, algorithmic literacy needs to teach calibration, not just content. Most digital literacy efforts focus on pouring in more information about how algorithms work. My findings suggest that’s only half the job. The other half is helping people accurately judge what they don’t know.

    Second, interventions should look different for different audiences. For younger, overconfident users, that might mean exercises designed to puncture false certainty: quick self-assessments that reveal the gap between what someone assumes and what they can actually explain, or interactive demonstrations of common misconceptions about how feeds are built. For older, underconfident users, the goal isn’t to manufacture confidence. It’s to help them recognize the caution they already bring to online information as a genuine strength, and to pair it with the skills to tell trustworthy sources from untrustworthy ones, so that skepticism becomes discernment rather than disengagement.

    Third, anyone trying to reach audiences through algorithmic platforms, from educators to newsrooms to the platforms themselves, should stop assuming that the youngest people are the savviest. Confidence and competence are different things, and treating one as a proxy for the other leaves both groups poorly served.

    The next time a young adult confidently explains “how the algorithm works,” it might be worth asking: How can you be sure you actually know that? And the next time an older relative shrugs and states they don’t think they get it, it might be just another kind of miscalibration — with costs of its own, just a quieter one.

    Myojung Chung is an associate professor of journalism and media innovation at Northeastern University and a faculty associate at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society at Harvard University.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
    • It has been revealed that most Kit creators don't have a dedicated Creator Growth Manager, and when their emails start landing in spam, they need someone who can find the cause swiftly and explain it in plain language.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    It has been revealed that most Kit creators don't have a dedicated Creator Growth Manager, and when their emails start landing in spam, they need someone who can find the cause swiftly and explain it in plain language. We're looking for a Deliverability and Compliance Specialist to own deliverability support for that long tail of creators, run Kit's abuse desk, and make the compliance calls that protect the sending reputation every creator on Kit shares.

    In a recent development, you'll also build the playbooks, training, and AI-assisted workflows that help Support and contractors handle more deliverability questions on their own, and you'll partner with our infrastructure engineers as we run more of our sending in-house. A creator can't build a lasting business if their emails don't arrive, so this work connects directly to our mission.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes digging through headers and bounce logs to find the real cause of a problem, can explain DMARC alignment to a first-time creator without jargon, and is comfortable making a firm call when a situation is gray. You don't wait for someone to tell you what needs fixing. You proactively spot opportunities, identify patterns, and take the initiative to improve deliverability before problems arise.

    You'll report to Alyssa Dulin, Director of Creator Success, and collaborate closely with:.

    Our Deliverability team: a Deliverability Lead who supports our highest-value accounts and leads deliverability education, and a Deliverability Specialist who onboards and ramps up large senders moving to Kit.

    Our infrastructure engineers, who run Kit's sending infrastructure.

    Our compliance and anti-abuse engineers, who build the automated checks that keep spammers off Kit.

    Product Specialists and the Support team, who handle the front line and escalate deliverability problems to you.

    Customer Success Managers (we call them Creator Growth Managers at Kit), Sales and Migrations, and Product Managers.

    Recent findings suggest that first Week: Get set up in Kit, our admin tools, and our support and ticketing systems, and meet our distributed team in Get To Know You chats (GTKYs). Meet the deliverability team and get an introduction on the current projects. Read our deliverability playbooks and SOPs, and get access to the monitoring tools you'll use every day: Google Postmaster Tools, Microsoft SNDS, blocklist monitoring, and our internal delivery dashboards.

    In a recent development, first Month: Shadow the Deliverability team and Product Specialists on deliverability tickets, account approvals, and abuse reports, then start answering queue tickets with review. Join the daily monitoring rotation (blocklist delisting, Postmaster and delivery monitoring) and the weekly Deliverability team meeting. Learn how account approvals, compliance flags, and our in-house sending platform work. By the end of the month, work deliverability tickets and abuse reports on your own and send your first delisting requests. Project: build a recurring report showing the trending deliverability ticket reasons so we understand what’s causing how to reduce friction for customers and how to solve it.

    Industry observers note that first Six Months: Own the deliverability support queue for creators without a dedicated CGM: spam-folder placement, bounces, authentication and DMARC setup, and escalations from Product Specialists. Own compliance end to end, from new-account approvals and compliance flags to pausing or closing accounts that put our shared reputation at risk.Run Kit's abuse desk. You'll write and share a strategy that covers coverage, response-time targets, escalation paths, and quality checks, then put it in place so routine spam, phishing, and blocklist reports follow clear SOPs while you take the hardest cases yourself. Be the go-to contact for day-to-day mailbox provider concerns with Microsoft, Gmail, Yahoo, Comcast, and regional providers, and write an incident runbook for blocklistings and provider throttling. Track the queue with a simple scorecard (volume, first response time, and escalation rate) and share what you learn with the team. Run training sessions for Support and ship your first process or AI improvements, like cleaner ticket categorization or better account data for our AI support agent, so more deliverability tickets get solved without escalation..

    First Year: Deliverability support is faster and more consistent for every creator on Kit, including the ones who never talk to a CGM. Your playbooks, help center articles, and AI-assisted workflows are what Support, CGMs, and contractors reach for first, and fewer tickets need to come to you. You've led at least one cross-team fix with infrastructure for a recurring problem you spotted in the queue, such as an alert when a creator's domain authentication breaks or a check for sudden signup spikes. You're helping shape the internal tooling and alerting our in-house sending needs, and you take part in industry groups like M3AAWG.

    Deep working knowledge of email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, alignment, and BIMI basics), plus the ability to read raw message headers and SMTP bounce and deferral codes.

    Hands-on use of Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS/JMRP, and comfort working with major blocklists (Spamhaus, Abusix, Barracuda, Spamcop, and others) and their delisting processes.

    Data fluency: you can pull bounce, complaint, and engagement data together, find the root cause, and explain it so others can act on it.

    Hands-on abuse handling: you can work an abuse report or escalation start to finish, from finding the account and assessing the evidence to acting, replying to the reporter, and documenting the decision.

    Process building: you can turn repeat work into SOPs, playbooks, and quality checks that a contractor or teammate can follow.

    Clear, calm written communication with creators, teammates, and postmasters.

    Using AI tools to research, summarize, and draft, and helping teammates do the same, with the judgment to keep a person on final compliance calls.

    Experience with MTA logs or delivery observability tools (KumoMTA, PowerMTA, Postfix, Kibana/Elasticsearch, or SQL and BI tools like Mode).

    Familiarity with feedback loops, spam traps, list bombing, and bot-signup patterns.

    Familiarity with CAN-SPAM, CASL, and GDPR as they apply to marketing email.

    Experience with Intercom, HubSpot, or a similar ticketing tool.

    Experience building or tuning AI support workflows or macros.

    4+ years in email deliverability, compliance, trust and safety, or technical support at an ESP, mailbox provider, or high-volume sender.

    Handling escalated customer tickets end to end, including with customers who are frustrated.

    Making account-level compliance or abuse decisions, such as approving, suspending, or closing accounts.

    Working an abuse desk or abuse mailbox directly: spam and phishing complaints, provider and blocklist reports, and escalations.

    Leading the fix for a recurring deliverability or compliance problem that needed help from more than one team.

    Supporting senders on shared IP pools at an ESP.

    Setting abuse or trust and safety strategy, or directing contractors or vendors on a support or abuse queue.

    Working directly with mailbox provider postmaster teams.

    Participating in M3AAWG or other industry groups.

    Creating educational content, like help docs, training, workshops, or podcasts.

    Working with creators, digital entrepreneurs, or small businesses.

    You pick up problems that fall between teams without waiting for permission, and you follow them through until they're closed.

    You test a hypothesis against the evidence before you act, and you frame problems clearly enough that others trust your analysis.

    You protect the reputation every creator shares while staying fair and kind to the creator in front of you, and you help them understand the reasoning behind a decision.

    You turn what you learn into docs, templates, and training that others use, and you adjust how you teach to fit the audience.

    You hold a high bar for your work, and you push back respectfully, with data, when something puts our reputation at risk, even when Sales or leadership would prefer a different answer.

    You share in-progress work and risks early so the team can solve problems together.

    Treating deliverability as a set of macros rather than an investigation that needs judgment.

    Discomfort saying no to a creator or a teammate when our shared reputation is at stake.

    Waiting for someone to assign you work when you can already see the problem.

    Needing a fixed playbook, since our sending stack and processes are changing as we bring more sending in-house.

    Keeping knowledge in your head instead of writing it down for the next person.

    Preferring to work without AI tools.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe.     Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Sources indicate that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Many publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers.

    One of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The upcoming bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, and MarketWatch.

    Recent findings suggest that as part of the shift, the manufacturer revised each site’s robots.txt file — a webpage that tells bots which parts of a site they can and can’t access. Rather than reactively blacklisting bots through robots.txt, Dow Jones now operates with a whitelist for select crawlers and scrapers.

    Recent findings suggest that “As bot traffic has shifted from discovery-oriented use cases toward systems that can ingest, summarize, or otherwise benefit from our content without a relationship in place, we have moved to a more deliberate signal,” mentioned Nolly Evans, chief development officer at Dow Jones. “[This] signals to third parties that they must negotiate and partner directly with us for content access.”.

    The Wall Street Journal’s whitelist contains more than 60 bots, including search engine crawlers and three scrapers operated by OpenAI, which has a $250 million-plus licensing deal with Dow Jones’ parent tech giant, News Corp.

    “We’re seeing astronomical growth in bot traffic while human referrals and traffic to news sites are being curtailed,” said Evans. “That’s a clear signal to publishers that the old norms are no longer working, and that something needs to change.”.

    It has been revealed that robots.txt files are voluntary guidance for all bots, including those deployed by AI companies. They’re not hard technical blocks or legally binding contracts. Some AI companies, like Perplexity, have used “stealth crawlers” to bypass robots.txt files while evading detection. Still, The Journal isn’t alone in using robots.txt to disallow bots by default, whether to create friction for scrapers, as leverage to negotiate for content licensing deals, or to minimize the burden on their servers.

    An analysis of the robots.txt files of 1,000 leading English-language publishers websites by the bot analytics company Known Agents highlights that about 2% of those sites now disallow all bots by default, including Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Publishers Weekly, and the British technology news site The Register.

    Many of these publications are owned by News Corp, including several of the firm’s Australian newspapers (The Australian, The Daily Telegraph in Sydney, the Herald Sun in Melbourne) and its marquee U.K. papers (The Times, The Sun, The Scottish Sun).

    Industry observers note that “One of the most key concerns for us is making sure that the IP journalists create is respected by the AI companies,” News Corp CEO Robert Thomson remarked in an interview with CNBC last week. “The principled companies want to have an agreement, and the unprincipled companies don’t. We’ll try to convince you to be transactional and pay us for our IP and pay us for our journalism, or we’ll sue you.”.

    More and more publishers are opting to restrict bots using whitelists. Late last year, The Atlantic told Digiday that it only allows bots associated with its licensing deals or those that drive significant traffic to the website. In June, Digiday first reported that Reuters and Time had started issuing whitelists of their own.

    People Inc. has been vocal about its decision to go beyond robots.txt files and hard-block bots by default. When the manufacturer made the switch at the beginning of this year, it went from blocking 2,000 unique bots to more than 30,000.

    Industry observers note that many of these publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers. Over the past 90 days, around 34% of pageviews across more than 5,000 randomly selected websites came from bots, according to an index maintained by Known Agents. About 29% of those bots were “AI-related” (e.g. AI agents, AI chatbots, and AI training scrapers), as opposed to more traditional bots like search engine crawlers and archivers operated by the Wayback Machine.

    Despite some publishers wanting to restrict AI-related bot traffic, many aren’t making full use of their robots.txt files to do so, according to Gavin King, the CEO of Known Agents. The company started as a free crowdsourced database to help identify bots, but now offers publishers analytic tools and other products to monitor and control bot traffic.

    Known Agents right now tracks more than 2,000 AI-related bots, but the majority of English-language news publishers only restrict a fraction of those on their robots.txt files.

    In a recent development, “Robots.txt is the easiest first line of defense,” mentioned King. “The fact that people are reaching out to [internet infrastructure companies to sign] six-figure year contracts instead of updating their robots.txt for free is such a miss.”.

    Sources indicate that king acknowledged that robots.txt alone can’t stop content from being scraped without permission or compensation. But he also pointed to clients who have reduced traffic from known AI-related bots by more than 90% by updating their robots.txt file with a more comprehensive list.

    Industry observers note that “It’s been such a manual process,” said King. “Everyone is doing it individually, in-house instead of automating the process.”.

    Sources indicate that slate is one of the publications that has leaned on Known Agents’ “Automated Robots.txt” to try to stem the tide of AI bots to its site. Slate’s small product team uses the free version of the tool to access Known Agents’ API weekly and review any newly discovered bots or renamed agents that have been added to the manufacturer’s database. The tool automatically revises its robots.txt file based on that review.

    In a recent development, “We have almost 30 years of content, which is a long history of being online,” Greg Lavallee, Slate’s VP of technology, said. “We’re seeing no value from bots and it costs us bandwidth fees, so we decided to tell them not to bother.”.

    Lavallee noted that since September, preliminary data shows that several bots have ignored the publication’s robots.txt and continue to attempt to crawl its website, though he declined to name the exact bots. Slate is exploring “server-side paywall strategies that will make it more difficult for scrapers to access full content,” he remarked.

    Slate right now has no licensing deals with major AI companies, despite active outreach to buyers in the past.

    “It’s very easy for us to take that robots.txt list and go look at the [server] logs and say, ‘We told you not to access and then you did,” said Lavallee. “I feel like you have to [update your Robots.txt file], but it’s definitely not enough. Something more needs to happen than asking nicely.”.

    In a recent development, kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    According to recent reports, our Sales team needs a dedicated data partner, and creator commerce (how creators monetize by selling digital products) is becoming a bigger part of how Kit and our creators scale. Kit is growing, so we're looking for a Senior Analytics Engineer to own Kit's sales and commerce data from end to end.

    Sources indicate that accurate sales data gives our team a clear picture of the pipeline and the confidence to make informed decisions. That’s what makes this role so important.

    It has been revealed that your primary focus will be Sales: the dbt models that turn our CRM data into trusted pipeline, deal, and funnel metrics, and the Omni dashboards our sales leader and Senior Revenue Operations Manager use to run the business. You'll also model creator commerce data, so we understand what creators sell and earn through Kit, and you'll pick up reporting work with our Product team, such as feature usage reporting. On a small data team, we step outside our usual lanes when the need is there, so the mix will shift over time.

    It has been revealed that you'll build for two kinds of consumers: people and AI. Teammates increasingly answer their own questions by querying our semantic layer through Omni's AI and MCP connections to AI tools. That means your models, metric definitions, and documentation need to be clear and correct enough for an AI agent to use them without a data teammate in the loop.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes being close to the business, enjoys turning messy operational data into numbers people trust, and is happy to work on both the models and the dashboards that sit on top of them. When Sales and Product have clear, reliable data, we help more creators build more valuable businesses with Kit.

    You'll report to Sam Umachi, Head of Data (Linkedin).

    Recent findings suggest that sales and RevOps are your primary partners, who will rely on the models and reporting you own. You'll also partner with our Product team on reporting for features like Visual Automations and on how creators use Kit.

    Within our data team, you'll work alongside a Staff Analytics Engineer who owns org-wide semantic layer governance and modeling standards, a Senior Data Engineer who owns ingestion and pipelines, and a Senior Business Analytics Partner focused on revenue opportunities. This role has no direct reports.

    According to recent reports, first Week: Work through our onboarding curriculum in Notion and meet the data team, our Senior Revenue Operations Manager, the sales team, and your product partners. Get set up in our core tools: dbt Cloud, GitHub, Amazon Redshift, Omni, HubSpot, Linear, Hightouch and Slack. Set up your AI-assisted development environment and learn the shared AI workflows our data team uses. Open and merge your first small pull request so you learn our review and deployment flow early.

    In a recent development, first Month: Map how HubSpot objects (deals, pipelines and stages, companies, contacts, and owners) flow into our dbt models, and document the gaps. Take over day-to-day ownership of the sales models and Omni dashboards that teammates have been covering. Audit current sales reporting and list where definitions differ or numbers don't reconcile. Get familiar with how commerce data (products creators sell and the revenue they earn through Kit) lands in the warehouse today. Agree with RevOps and Sales on the most important questions they need answered. Review teammates' pull requests and contribute to our shared SQL, dbt, and documentation standards. Share a written reflection with the team on what you've learned and where you'd focus first.

    First Six Months: Ship and maintain well-tested, documented dbt models for core sales metrics, such as pipeline, deal velocity, stage conversion, win rates, and the sales-led funnel. Expose those metrics through the Omni semantic layer, working within the team's governance standards. Rebuild or refresh the core sales dashboards so pipeline reviews and forecasting conversations run on numbers that don't need manual reconciliation. Resolve competing sales metric definitions by writing down the options and tradeoffs, aligning with Sales and RevOps, and documenting the outcome. Model creator-level commerce data, such as products sold, revenue earned through Kit, and conversion, in partnership with data engineering. Write semantic layer descriptions, metric definitions, and documentation that let Omni's AI and MCP-connected AI tools answer routine sales questions correctly, and test them against real questions from Sales, RevOps and Product. Get Sales to the point where routine questions are answered through self-serve, whether in Omni dashboards, Omni's AI, or AI tools connected over MCP, rather than one-off requests.

    First Year: Be the recognized owner of Kit's sales data, the person Sales and RevOps go to first and trust without second-guessing. Give our revenue analysis work the sales and commerce models it depends on, so deeper questions about pipeline health and creator earnings can be answered quickly, thereby enabling us to make creators more successful. Leave your domains well documented and well tested, legible to fresh teammates, stakeholders, and the AI agents that query our semantic layer. Help raise the team's modeling quality through code review, pairing, and sharing what you learn.

    Deep dbt experience. You build modular, tested, documented dbt projects, and you're comfortable with incremental models, snapshots, macros, CI, and scheduled jobs in dbt Cloud or similar.

    Advanced SQL. You reason carefully about grain, joins, and window functions, and you write queries that are readable and performant on a cloud warehouse.

    According to recent reports, data modeling for sales and GTM. You can model deals, pipeline stages and their history, ownership changes, and funnel conversion into clean, reusable structures. You are opinionated on Kimball standards and when a concept should be a fact or dimension.

    CRM data fluency. You know how sales data behaves in a CRM, including stage changes, backdated edits, and custom properties. HubSpot is preferred, but other CRM experience (e.g. Salesforce) applies just as well. We care most that you recognize common CRM patterns.

    Working on a small or remote team where you were trusted to make decisions independently.

    Industry observers note that ownership and follow-through. You treat your data domains as yours. You notice problems before stakeholders do, close the loop on requests, and finish what you start.

    Industry observers note that judgment. You match rigor to the decision at hand, know when a quick answer is enough and when a request should become a durable model, and say so clearly.

    Industry observers note that flexibility. You're glad to step outside your primary area when another team needs help, and you balance that work against your core commitments openly.

    Teach everything you know. You document as you go, pair generously, and help stakeholders understand the data well enough to use it on their own.

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that openAI doesn’t initiative to provide ChatGPT advertisers with reports showing the prompts or inferred intent behind their ads.
    • Recent findings suggest that three executives who run OpenAI’s ad system told Adweek that ChatGPT ads are matched to search queries written by the tech giant’s own AI agent.
    • OpenAI’s basics page for advertisers explains that Ads Manager Beta reporting at the moment includes impressions, clicks, spend, CTR, average CPC, average CPM and conversions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that openAI doesn’t initiative to provide ChatGPT advertisers with reports showing the prompts or inferred intent behind their ads. When Adweek asked whether advertisers could expect such reports, Vijaye Raji, OpenAI’s CTO of applications, mentioned they should not expect them.

    Recent findings suggest that three executives who run OpenAI’s ad system told Adweek that ChatGPT ads are matched to search queries written by the tech giant’s own AI agent. Advertisers don’t see those queries, only aggregate results.

    OpenAI’s basics page for advertisers explains that Ads Manager Beta reporting at the moment includes impressions, clicks, spend, CTR, average CPC, average CPM and conversions.

    OpenAI’s “About this ad” panel tells owners why they saw an ad and what performance data advertisers receive.

    Industry observers note that openAI’s ad system begins by creating one or more search queries based upon buying intent determined from the conversation, per the company’s ads engineering post published Oct. 21 by Ritendra Datta and Karthik Gopalratnam. OpenAI calls the model that creates these search queries the orchestrator. Using these search queries, the ad system retrieves candidate ads, filters them, scores them and identifies the top candidates to be entered into an auction to set the price and select the winner. Returning no ad is called “an ordinary, successful outcome” in the post.

    As described in the post, if a user asks about a two-day Yosemite trip and then about a shoe brand’s new product lines, the ad system may create a query representing that conversation such as “shoes appropriate for hiking trip,” even though the user did not connect the two questions.

    According to the post, when ads personalization is turned on, the orchestrator will also consider “nonsensitive information about the user’s past conversations.”.

    ChatGPT people in the European Economic Area and Switzerland will not have access to personalized ads at first, according to OpenAI’s ads FAQ for users. Brooke Osmundson covered the engineering post in October.

    Advertisers share context hints about where an ad might fit, and OpenAI notes these hints help guide matching without determining it.

    OpenAI’s context hints guide says:.

    “Hints are not targeting rules or delivery instructions. They do not guarantee that your ad will appear for particular conversations, audiences, or situations, and they cannot enforce geographic limits, schedules, or exclusions.”.

    The basics page also indicates that hints “are not exact-match keywords.” Negative Phrases help qualifying advertisers limit where their ads appear, for “narrow placement requirements specific to their brand’s own policies.” The option is not necessarily available to every advertiser.

    Google explains that for some AI searches, the search terms provided in Google Ads reporting reflect the user’s intent rather than the exact query. According to Google’s ad group prioritization page, for searches done through Lens, AI Mode, AI Overviews and autocomplete, “the search term shown in your reporting represents the best approximation of the user’s intent.” Brooke posted about Google’s update to that page in May.

    OpenAI does not list a search terms report on its basics page.

    ChatGPT advertisers can determine what a campaign delivered, but they cannot see the conversations or queries that led to the results. Click-based and conversion-based campaigns can use the conversion tracking OpenAI supports through Ads Manager Beta. The basics page also describes how UTM parameters added to landing page URLs persist on ad clicks.

    OpenAI recommends writing your context hints in terms of customer needs and scenarios instead of listing keywords. Also, use OpenAI’s product controls where available to restrict delivery by geography.

    Recent findings suggest that openAI says in its ads FAQ for people that it “may explore additional measurement insights over time while continuing to protect user privacy.” OpenAI sends upcoming feature announcements by email to account holders. Check the reporting list on the basics page for updates.

    Industry News: What SEOs Can Be Thankful For: 8 Wins To Celebrate In 2026 via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that in SEO, we like to complain, but this industry and craft is also about finding the small wins to celebrate.
    • Recent findings suggest that search may have given us plenty to navigate this year in AI, but Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI were each able to find their own ways to offer up some AI visibility.
    • This article is the Search Engine Journal Thanksgiving list for all things SEO, social, local, and PPC.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that in SEO, we like to complain, but this industry and craft is also about finding the small wins to celebrate. Today is a day to consider what we are thankful for, so let us dig deep and create our SEO Thanksgiving list.

    Recent findings suggest that search may have given us plenty to navigate this year in AI, but Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI were each able to find their own ways to offer up some AI visibility. We can take the crumbs.

    This article is the Search Engine Journal Thanksgiving list for all things SEO, social, local, and PPC. We finish off with a celebration for anybody who clicked their back button and went somewhere they had never been before.

    Google Search Console is currently displaying dedicated reports for your impressions in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and generative AI features in Discover, by page, country, and date. These latest reports were released in June, and Google’s announcement now states, “As of August 31, 2026, we’ve rolled out these insights to all websites worldwide.”.

    We’re glad to finally see the AI impressions separated out from the normal impression totals.

    SEJ covered it here: Google Search Console AI Reports Rolled Out Worldwide.

    Microsoft Bing Webmaster Tools added an AI performance report in February as a public preview, showing how many times Microsoft Copilot, Bing’s AI summarizations, and some partner integrations reference your content, along with the referenced pages and the grounding query (the phrase used by the AI to retrieve the content).

    It has been revealed that in June, Microsoft added a Citation Share feature in preview, which provides insight into what percentage of citations for a grounding query go to your site. The February report gives you a count of how many times you appeared in the citation list, and Citation Share reveals how large a piece of the pie those citations represent.

    SEJ covered it here: Bing Webmaster Tools Adds AI Citation Performance Data and here Google Search Console AI Reports Rolled Out Worldwide.

    It has been revealed that on Nov. 10, OpenAI released ChatGPT Business Hub in beta. All eligible businesses where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in Business Hub and, after claims and identity verification are approved, will be able to see mentions, website clicks, and discovery topics over the past 28 days.

    According to OpenAI’s setup guide for online businesses, a mention occurs when ChatGPT references your website, not if it just names your brand.

    Vahan Petrosyan, director of technology for SEJ, submitted Search Engine Journal, and Business Hub demonstrated 353,356 mentions and 2,663 website clicks from Oct. 14 through Nov. 10.

    SEJ’s mentions and website clicks from Oct. 14 through Nov. 10. Screenshot by Vahan Petrosyan, Search Engine Journal.

    This is a beta version, and OpenAI notes that claiming a business does not assure greater visibility within ChatGPT. However, these numbers are provided directly from ChatGPT, and mentions cannot be reflected in referral reports.

    SEJ covered it here: How to Submit Your Website to ChatGPT Business Hub.

    Industry observers note that google introduced platform properties for social and video accounts in July and made them available to everybody worldwide on July 29. They provide information regarding clicks, impressions, CTR and average position for posts on Instagram, TikTok, X and YouTube appearing in Google Search. Reports for Discover and Google News will also be displayed when applicable.

    Recent findings suggest that the Insights report for a YouTube platform property shows clicks from Google Search over 28 days. Source: Google Search Central (CC BY 4.0, cropped).

    Your social team can now track how users locate the team’s social content on Google Search, within Search Console, the same tool utilized by your SEO team.

    SEJ covered it here: Google Search Console Adds Reports For Social Posts.

    In a recent development, google announced the branded queries filter last November and made it available to all eligible sites by March. The branded queries filter allows you to sort your Performance report queries into branded, including misspellings, and non-branded, so you can identify traffic coming from users searching specifically for your brand or products.

    The Search Analytics API got the same branded split this month. Prior to this branded queries filter being implemented, tracking traffic based upon specific branded searches required “maintaining complex keyword regex lists,” as Google put it. Many will agree that it is refreshing to no longer need such lists.

    SEJ covered it here: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API.

    Google’s September Small Business Bulletin described view counts for Business Profile posts as “currently rolling out globally.”.

    Once the rollout has completed for your Business Profile, each post card located under the dashboard section will indicate views generated from Search and Maps activity for posts from the past 18 months.

    Google removed post metrics from Business Profiles in 2023. Now you can determine which posts receive the most views rather than making educated guesses. However, the bulletin mentioned the counts were not accessible via the API yet.

    SEJ covered it here: Google Adds Post View Counts To Business Profiles.

    For PPC advertisers working in TikTok Ads Manager, the Q4 product preview highlighted Impression Share, a common metric seen in Google Ads, along with Top 1 Impression Share for Search Ads campaigns.

    It has been revealed that impression Share measures the percentage of eligible search results impressions that your ads capture. According to TikTok’s help section, availability of Impression Share may vary depending on account and market. Still, it can quickly reveal what portion of eligible search visibility you are leaving behind.

    TikTok also added Keyword Packs (pre-made brand and category keywords) to the Keyword Suggestion Tool for a faster way to create keyword lists.

    SEJ covered it here: TikTok Search Ads Adds Brand And Category Keyword Packs.

    Google began treating back button hijacking as a malicious practice in April and started enforcing this policy on June 15. Sites using back button hijacking could be subject to either a manual action or automated demotion.

    On Nov. 23, Google released a upcoming FAQ which claims the policy will apply if the back button hijacking occurs in a user’s browser, including when they visit your page via social media. Although this policy cannot eliminate all cases of back button hijacking, websites presently utilizing this tactic may want to stop.

    SEJ covered it here: Google Claims Back Button Hijacking Policy Covers Social Visits.

    According to recent reports, our single request for next year’s Thanksgiving holiday is the ability to differentiate Search Console’s AI clicks from web clicks. Right now, every time someone clicks on an AI Overview or AI Mode link, that click counts in the same Performance report as clicks on your other search engine results.

    Happy Thanksgiving from all the SEJ team.

    Featured Image: Zamrznuti tonovi/Shutterstock.

    #148073. Tech Report: The Missing Step In Prompt Tracking Was Written Down In 1995 via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1983 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: The Missing Step In Prompt Tracking Was Written Down In 1995 via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The AI visibility industry has worked out how many prompts to track and how often to run them, and it still has no method for deciding which questions belong in the set or what a correct answer to any of them would be.
    • In a recent development, over the last year, the sampling side of prompt tracking has matured rapidly.
    • Sources indicate that what has not matured is the step before sampling.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The AI visibility industry has worked out how many prompts to track and how often to run them, and it still has no method for deciding which questions belong in the set or what a correct answer to any of them would be. That second problem is older than the first, and it has a documented solution that predates Google. Knowledge engineers have used it since the mid-1990s under the name competency questions, and it is almost absent from the conversation in search.

    In a recent development, over the last year, the sampling side of prompt tracking has matured rapidly. Practitioners now broadly accept that a single run of a single prompt tells you very little, that branded and unbranded prompts have to be reported separately, and that wording changes results. The research supports the caution. A peer-reviewed study presented at ICLR 2024 found that formatting changes alone, with the meaning of the prompt untouched, moved one open-source model’s accuracy by as much as 76 points on standard benchmark tasks. That study tested benchmarks, not brands, but it establishes the underlying behavior: These systems respond to the form of a question as well as its content.

    Sources indicate that what has not matured is the step before sampling. A scoping review posted this fall examined 38 empirical studies that query language models and measure outcomes for brands, and it judged that only five of them could defend how their prompts were chosen. Most used prompts written by the authors or generated by a model, with no evidence that those prompts represent what buyers ask. A separate survey makes the consequence plain: the prompts you pick, and the weight you give each one, define the market your visibility score describes, and that market may not match real demand. Both papers are preprints from single authors and have not been through peer review, so I treat them as a careful reading of the field and not as final findings.

    The same review found that authors with a commercial stake in visibility services, or in a brand being measured, were behind 19 of those 38 studies. I am one of those people, since I founded CitationIQ, which measures AI visibility, and you should weigh what follows with that understanding (I was not part of any of those studies, for the record).

    The practical result is familiar to anyone who has sat in a prompt-selection meeting or had to choose them. Someone opens a spreadsheet, the team brainstorms questions, a tool suggests a few hundred more, and the list is frozen so that next month’s number can be compared with this month’s. Nobody writes down why each prompt is there, what business situation it stands for, or what the model would have to say for the answer to count as right. The score that comes out is precise, and its meaning is undefined.

    It has been revealed that in the early 1990s, Michael Grüninger and Mark Fox at the University of Toronto were building formal models of how enterprises operate, and they needed a way to decide what a model had to contain before anyone built it. Their answer, published in 1995, was to start with the situations the model had to support and then write the questions it must be able to answer in those situations. They called these competency questions because the questions define what the model is competent to do.

    Sources indicate that the thing they were building is called an ontology, which is easiest to relate to the knowledge graph you already know. The graph holds the facts, and the ontology is the blueprint those facts are organized by: what kinds of things exist, what properties they carry, and how they can relate. Schema.org plays that role for structured data on the web. Most entity work fills in the graph without stating what it must be able to answer, which is the gap competency questions close. From here on I will call the ontology a knowledge model.

    Sources indicate that A competency question is a question a knowledge model must be able to answer, written down before the model is built and used afterward to test whether it works. The questions come first, they come from real situations, and they double as the acceptance test. The Toronto method ran in six stages: Describe the motivating scenarios, write the questions informally, define the terms, restate the questions formally, write the rules, and then establish the conditions under which the model answers the questions completely. Later researchers borrowed test-first development from software engineering and turned the questions into tests that are written before the model is changed.

    Set that beside the spreadsheet. The knowledge engineer can trace every question to a scenario and every test to a question. The prompt list has no scenarios behind it and no expected answers in front of it.

    It would be convenient to say that knowledge engineers solved this and marketers only need to copy them, and it would be wrong. A 2023 survey of 63 ontology engineers found that most of them use competency questions routinely, and that 77.8% have difficulty making sure their questions are both necessary and sufficient. Nearly two-thirds have trouble identifying questions that truly represent the scope, about half have trouble writing them properly, and two-thirds work with no guideline at all. Other researchers note that teams rarely publish their questions alongside the finished model, which means the requirements are often lost.

    It has been revealed that I find that reassuring, not discouraging. Thirty years of practice has produced a clear record of where the method breaks: vague questions, questions nobody can check, question sets that drift away from the scenarios that justified them, and requirements that live in one person’s head. Those are the failures a prompt list has today, and the knowledge engineering literature has names and partial remedies for each of them. One recent classification separates scoping questions, which mark out what a model should cover, from validating questions, which check whether what it states is correct. That split maps directly onto the two things a brand wants to know: whether it appears in the answer at all, and whether what the answer says about it is true.

    The method does not transfer whole, and the reason matters. A knowledge model is deterministic: you run the formal query, and it returns the answer, or it does not. A language model is probabilistic, so the same question produces different answers across runs, phrasings, and engines, and the result is a rate instead of a pass or fail. You also do not own the thing being tested. A knowledge engineer who finds a failed question fixes the model, while you can only change the material the model draws on.

    According to recent reports, my adaptation, which is my own extension and not something the literature prescribes, is to run each competency question as two tests in a fixed order. First test your own content, which is deterministic: can a person find the expected answer, stated plainly, on a page you control or in a source you can influence? That is a pass or a fail, and you can fix a fail yourself. Only then test the language model by asking the question in several phrasings, several times, across the engines your buyers use, and recording how often the expected answer comes back. A critical survey of GEO research recommends three to five phrasings per information need, which is a sensible floor.

    According to recent reports, the order matters because a language model that fails a question your own content cannot answer has told you nothing about the language model. In an earlier piece, I argued that AI visibility is three separate problems on three layers, and this is the diagnostic step that tells you which layer to look at. It also clarifies the relationship between a question and a prompt. The competency question is the requirement and the prompts are test cases for it, so twenty phrasings of one question are still one requirement, and a list of three hundred prompts may cover far fewer needs than it appears to.

    Industry observers note that to make this concrete, take DuaneRoll, a payroll software tech giant I invented for this article. It sells to businesses with 50 to 500 employees, and its motivating scenario is a finance leader whose company has just hired in a third state and who asks an AI assistant what to do about payroll. Here are five competency questions for it.

    Recent findings suggest that the fifth question is the one most prompt lists lack. An AI answer that credits you with a service you do not offer creates a support problem at best, and as I wrote about the German court rulings, an answer built from accurate facts attached to the wrong firm can become a legal one. Testing for what should not be mentioned is as much a requirement as testing for what should.

    It has been revealed that notice what the bad question has in common with most tracked prompts. It sounds like something a buyer would ask, it produces an answer every time, and the answer can be scored for sentiment. It fails as a requirement because there is nothing to check it against.

    Every expected answer above has a named owner, and that is deliberate. In knowledge engineering, a domain expert stands behind each expected answer. A prompt test usually has no such person, and the result gets pasted into a report with no record of which model, which version, which date, or whether web search was on. Sascha Donner, writing this year in the Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, argues that text from a language model lacks the testimonial grounding documents have always had, and that it becomes a usable document only when a person fixes it in a form and takes responsibility for it. The same applies to a test result. An expected answer needs a witness, meaning a named person who will say it is correct, and a logged result needs its conditions recorded, or it is an anecdote with a percentage attached.

    Once the questions exist, most of the measurement decisions make themselves. Each question claims what to look for, each expected answer says what counts as correct, each owner says who to ask when the answer changes, and each scenario says why the question deserves a place in the set. Sampling, which the industry has learned to do well, then operates on a set that means something. A score built that way can be explained to a chief marketing officer in one sentence: Of the things buyers need to know about us, this is the share the engines get right.

    One caution before you hand the job to a machine. Asking an AI system to write your competency questions and grade the answers is tempting, and researchers are actively studying it. A study using 1,393 competency questions found that human evaluators’ performance dropped when the AI assistant gave them incorrect guidance. A language model can draft candidate questions quickly, and a person who knows the business still has to decide which ones are requirements.

    Industry observers note that A competency question set for a brand is a short, owned list of what buyers must be able to learn about you, each item traceable to a real buying situation and paired with an answer someone will vouch for. Start with 10. Write the scenario, the question, the expected answer, and the owner; check your own content first, and only then look at what the engines say. The method is thirty years old, its weaknesses are well documented, and it is still more than most prompt lists have behind them.

    This post was originally published on Duane Forrester Decodes.

    Recent findings suggest that you'll work closely with our Postgres engineering teams and with the PM lead for Databases, who leads Multigres. You'll define the Postgres requirements that architecture must meet, and own how customers experience their database through that transition.

    Recent findings suggest that you'll make maintenance predictable. You'll design how we schedule, communicate and run maintenance windows so customers stay informed and in control, and disruption is rare and expected.

    Recent findings suggest that you'll help developers understand their database. Query performance, metrics, logs and advisors: you'll own the path from "my database is slow" to the fix.

    Industry observers note that you'll own our extension ecosystem. Which extensions we offer, how we evaluate and support new ones, and how we keep them working across versions.

    You'll own Postgres security. Roles and permissions, Row Level Security ergonomics, secure defaults, and how we respond to Postgres and extension CVEs.

    You'll talk to developers across the full spectrum, from indie developers on their first project to enterprises running critical workloads, and bring what you learn into every prioritization call.

    You'll own the problem definition, requirements and success metrics for what we ship, such as upgrade success rate, the share of the fleet on supported versions, and time-to-diagnose for performance problems. You'll set the metric before the team builds, then track it after launch.

    Industry observers note that you'll keep Engineering, Support and GTM aligned. You'll own the strategy of record for what's coming, why, and in what order, and communicate version changes and deprecations clearly to customers.

    4+ years of Product Management experience on databases, developer tools or infrastructure, or equivalent depth as an engineer, DBA or founder moving into product. You're comfortable commenting on an architecture doc and advocating for the user when trade-offs are required.

    Know Postgres well, or another relational database well enough to ramp rapidly. You're comfortable reading EXPLAIN output and talking about replication, WAL, roles and extensions.

    Sources indicate that have shipped products where reliability and trust are the experience. You treat downtime and breaking changes as product problems, not just operational ones.
